## Start with a specific question

**LeetCode 1044 — Longest Duplicate Substring.** We will reason from a very small example rather than introduce a complicated notation first.

## What the obvious approach overlooks

Compare every pair of substrings; a length-n string has quadratic many substrings and their comparisons can be expensive.

## One simple idea

A suffix array sorts the starting positions of all suffixes. Repeated substrings become shared prefixes of neighbouring suffixes in lexicographic order.

Before reading symbols, explain the intended operation aloud. If you can say which information is saved and which work is avoided, you have the core intuition.

## Formula and immediate translation

$$
S[SA_0:]\leq_{\mathrm{lex}}\cdots\leq_{\mathrm{lex}}S[SA_{n-1}:]
$$

**Symbols and notation:** S is the input string of length n; SA_i is the starting index of the i-th suffix in sorted order; ≤_lex denotes lexicographic string order.

**Insert actual numbers:** For 'banana', suffix starting positions sort as [5,3,1,0,4,2]: 'a','ana','anana','banana','na','nana'. Adjacent 'ana' and 'anana' have common prefix 'ana' of length 3, revealing a repeated substring.

This numerical calculation is essential: the expression must mean the same thing when evaluated by hand and when written in code.

## Why the mathematics leads to an algorithm

Any two strings with a long shared prefix become clustered in a lexicographically ordered list. The longest repeated substring occurs in the longest common prefix of some adjacent sorted suffixes.

This argument is the bridge between 'the equation looks plausible' and 'the result is correct for all inputs satisfying the assumptions'.

## Make the idea executable

Start with the numerical example above and write a tiny function or test that reproduces it. For comparison, examine the [original executable patterns library](../examples/patterns.mjs). This topic's main challenge is its mathematical invariant rather than framework setup.

## Complexity and correctness boundaries

**Work bound:** Naive demonstration O(n² log n) character comparisons or worse depending on string comparisons; efficient suffix-array construction can be O(n log n) or O(n).

**Counterexample or limitation:** Building all suffix strings and sorting is pedagogically simple but uses O(n²) character storage; efficient suffix-array algorithms work on positions and have better bounds.

Always declare the input domain first. For example, a modulus must be positive, a probability denominator nonzero and a character indexing convention fixed. Many seemingly clever solutions fail because these conditions were never stated.
